scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance traces its lineage to the 11th-century 'Chavettu Pada' (suicide squads) of feudal Kerala, who were instrumental in the Chera-Chola wars.
These soldiers were known for their rigorous training and devotion to local deities.
While the martial movements are ancient, Parichamuttukali became a distinct dance form differentiated from other Kalari-based arts around the 16th century.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically performed as a religious offering, it is now a centerpiece of Syrian Christian entertainment.
It is commonly seen at church gatherings and during the secular festival of Onam.
The dance serves as a 'mock fight' (kali) rather than an actual combat (ankam), celebrating both martial prowess and religious faith.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers move in a circle around a central point, usually a Nilavilakku (oil lamp).
They carry wooden swords and shields, clashing them together in rhythm.
The footwork and body mechanics are derived from Kalarippayattu, featuring low-gravity stances and radial symmetry.
Watch for Paricha Muttuka, Kalari Steps.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is primarily vocal, performed as a chorus by the dancers themselves.
They are led by an Asan (chief) who often chimes bells to maintain the tempo.
Listen for the Bells (Ilathalam or similar), Wooden swords, Wooden shields.

The sound is dominated by the rhythmic, percussive 'clack' of wooden shields meeting, overlaid with a male vocal chorus singing folk melodies. The Asan’s bells provide a sharp, metallic pulse that drives the increasing tempo.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear a traditional white loincloth (dhoti/mundu) and red wristbands, a garb that evokes the historical attire of Kalari warriors.
The setting is typically a church courtyard or a festival stage.
A brass oil lamp (Nilavilakku) is placed in the center of the performance space to provide a focal point for the circular formation.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The central figure in any performance is the Asan, the chief or teacher who leads the singing, chimes the bells, and directs the choreography.
The dance is also historically associated with the Harijan community in Kerala.
The dance is currently most prominent in the central district of Palakkad, the southern districts of Kottayam and Ernakulam, and Malappuram in the north.
Parichamuttukali is closely related to Margam Kali, another Christian dance form of Kerala.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Parichamuttukali is parent of Kalarippayattu: The dance movements and steps are directly derived from this ancient martial art.
Parichamuttukali is sibling of Margam Kali: A closely related Christian dance form from the same region and community.
Parichamuttukali is related of Chavittu Nadakam: Another Christian performing art from Kerala, though more theatrical in nature.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Assume a low Kalarippayattu-style stance with knees bent and back straight.
Step 2: Hold the sword in the dominant hand and the shield in the other.
Footwork from the sources: Stepping patterns that maintain a circular path while allowing for lunges and retreats.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Step forward into the circle, clashing the shield against the partner's or the next dancer's shield.
Step 4: Execute a rhythmic retreat while maintaining the circular formation.
Drill: Shifting weight from left to right without raising the head level.
